formulations.label: Solution 100 units/mL (long-acting; pre-filled pen or cartridge)
formulations.note: The 100 units/mL pre-filled pen has its own UK SmPC (MHRA Products, licence PLGB 04668/0410), cited for the pen; most clinical statements here quote the 100 units/mL cartridge SmPC, whose wording was checked against the pen SmPC (same insulin and strength; only device, table layout and in-use storage differ). A 200 units/mL pen also exists: units shown need no conversion between strengths. Subcutaneous only; not intravenous, not intramuscular, not in pumps.

src.q: Tresiba 100 units/mL solution for injection in pre-filled pen One pre-filled pen contains 300 units of insulin degludec in 3 mL solution.
1 mL solution contains 100 units insulin degludec* (equivalent to 3.66 mg insulin degludec).
Subcutaneous use only.
The dose counter shows the number of units regardless of strength and no dose conversion should be done when transferring a patient to a new strength.
there is no need for dose conversion when transferring patients from the standard to high strength version or vice versa

brandPrescribing.t: Prescribe insulin by brand name (SPS, citing NICE guidance), and make sure the patient gets a device they have been trained to use. Where one brand comes in more than one strength or device, the brand name alone is not enough: also state the strength and device (SPS).

src.q: NICE guidance recommends insulins are prescribed by brand name.
It is important to ensure patients receive an administration device they have been trained to use.
Where a single insulin brand is available in multiple strengths or delivery devices, using only a brand name is insufficient.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Diabetes mellitus in adults, adolescents and children from 1 year.

src.q: Treatment of diabetes mellitus in adults, adolescents and children from the age of 1 year.

items.t: Prescribe by brand name and device; where a brand has several strengths or devices, also state strength and device (SPS). Any switch between brands or formulations should be under strict supervision; a dose change may be needed.

src.q: NICE guidance recommends insulins are prescribed by brand name.
It is important to ensure patients receive an administration device they have been trained to use.
Where a single insulin brand is available in multiple strengths or delivery devices, using only a brand name is insufficient.
Manufacturers advise any switch between brands or formulation of insulin should be done under strict supervision; a change in dose may be required.

items.t: Transfer to another type, brand or manufacturer of insulin must be under medical supervision; a dose change may be needed. Two strengths exist: check the label every time.

src.q: Transferring a patient to another type, brand or manufacturer of insulin must be done under medical supervision and may result in the need for a change in dosage.
to avoid accidental mix-ups between the two different strengths of Tresiba as well as other insulin products

items.t: Once daily at any time, preferably the same time each day; when that is not possible, timing is flexible but keep at least 8 hours between injections. Adjust the dose by fasting plasma glucose. 1 unit equals 1 IU human insulin, 1 unit glargine 100 units/mL or 1 unit detemir.

src.q: This medicinal product is a basal insulin for once-daily subcutaneous administration at any time of the day, preferably at the same time every day.
A minimum of 8 hours between injections should always be ensured.
It is recommended to optimise glycaemic control via dose adjustment based on fasting plasma glucose.
One (1) unit of insulin degludec corresponds to 1 international unit of human insulin, 1 unit of insulin glargine (100 units/mL), or 1 unit of insulin detemir.

items.t: Type 2 diabetes: start 10 units once daily, then adjust; can be used alone or with oral antidiabetics, GLP-1 receptor agonists and bolus insulin.

src.q: The recommended daily starting dose is 10 units followed by individual dosage adjustments.
can be administered alone or in any combination with oral antidiabetic medicinal products, GLP-1 receptor agonists and bolus insulin

items.t: Type 1 diabetes: once daily with mealtime short/rapid-acting insulin, then individual adjustment.

src.q: Tresiba is to be used once daily with mealtime insulin and requires subsequent individual dosage adjustments.

items.t: Switching: type 2 diabetes, unit-for-unit from once-daily basal insulin; consider a 20% reduction when coming from twice-daily basal insulin or glargine 300 units/mL. Type 1 diabetes: consider a 20% reduction of the previous basal dose. Monitor glucose closely during and after transfer.

src.q: changing the basal insulin to Tresiba can be done unit-to-unit based on the previous basal insulin dose followed by individual dosage adjustments
transferring to Tresiba from twice-daily basal insulin - transferring to Tresiba from insulin glargine (300 units/mL)
For patients with type 1 diabetes a dose reduction of 20% based on the previous basal insulin dose
Close glucose monitoring is recommended during the transfer and in the following weeks.

items.t: Missed dose: take it when remembered, then return to the usual once-daily schedule.

src.q: Patients who forget a dose are advised to take it upon discovery and then resume their usual once-daily dosing schedule.

items.t: Elderly: intensify glucose monitoring and adjust the dose individually.

src.q: Tresiba can be used in elderly. Glucose monitoring is to be intensified and the insulin dose adjusted on an individual basis

items.t: Can be used from 1 year; no clinical experience below 1 year. No experience with flexible dose timing in children. When switching basal insulin, consider reducing basal and bolus doses to limit hypoglycaemia.

src.q: This medicinal product can be used in adolescents and children from the age of 1 year (see section 5.1).
There is no clinical experience with the use of this medicinal product in children below the age of 1 year.
There is no clinical experience with flexibility in dosing time of Tresiba in children and adolescents.
dose reduction of basal and bolus insulin needs to be considered on an individual basis in order to minimise the risk of hypoglycaemia

items.t: Hypersensitivity to insulin degludec or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Must not be given intravenously (severe hypoglycaemia) or intramuscularly (changes absorption), and must not be used in pumps. Never draw it from a pen cartridge into a syringe.

src.q: Tresiba must not be administered intravenously as it may result in severe hypoglycaemia. This medicinal product must not be administered intramuscularly as it may change the absorption. This medicinal product must not be used in insulin infusion pumps.
patients and healthcare professionals should never use a syringe to draw the medicinal product from the cartridge in the pre-filled pen

items.t: Hypoglycaemia: missed meals, unplanned strenuous exercise or too high a dose. Warning symptoms may change or disappear. The long action may delay recovery from hypoglycaemia.

src.q: Omission of a meal or unplanned strenuous physical exercise may lead to hypoglycaemia.
As with other basal insulin products, the prolonged effect of Tresiba may delay recovery from hypoglycaemia.

items.t: Severe hyperglycaemia: give rapid-acting insulin. Inadequate dosing or stopping may cause diabetic ketoacidosis.

src.q: Administration of rapid-acting insulin is recommended in situations with severe hyperglycaemia.
Inadequate dosing and/or discontinuation of treatment in patients requiring insulin may lead to hyperglycaemia and potentially to diabetic ketoacidosis.

items.t: Infection and fever usually raise insulin needs; kidney, liver, adrenal, pituitary or thyroid disease may need dose changes.

src.q: Concomitant illness, especially infections and fever, usually increases the patient's insulin requirement.
Concomitant diseases in the kidney, liver or diseases affecting the adrenal, pituitary or thyroid gland may require changes in the insulin dose.

items.t: Abrupt improvement in control may temporarily worsen diabetic retinopathy.

src.q: Intensification of insulin therapy with abrupt improvement in glycaemic control may be associated with temporary worsening of diabetic retinopathy

items.t: Rotate injection sites; monitor blood glucose after moving to an unaffected site. With pioglitazone: watch for heart failure, weight gain and oedema.

src.q: Patients must be instructed to perform continuous rotation of the injection site to reduce the risk of developing lipodystrophy and cutaneous amyloidosis.
If the combination is used, patients should be observed for signs and symptoms of heart failure, weight gain and oedema.

items.t: Patients must be able to read the dose counter; blind or poorly sighted patients need help from a trained person.

src.q: Patients who are blind or have poor vision must be instructed to always get help/assistance from another person who has good vision and is trained in using the insulin device.

items.t: May lower the insulin requirement (hypoglycaemia): oral antidiabetics, GLP-1 receptor agonists, MAOIs, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, salicylates, anabolic steroids, sulfonamides.

src.q: Oral antidiabetic medicinal products, GLP-1 receptor agonists, monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOI), beta-blockers, angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, salicylates, anabolic steroids and sulfonamides.

items.t: May raise the insulin requirement: oral contraceptives, thiazides, glucocorticoids, thyroid hormones, sympathomimetics, growth hormone, danazol.

src.q: Oral contraceptives, thiazides, glucocorticoids, thyroid hormones, sympathomimetics, growth hormone and danazol.

items.t: Beta-blockers may mask hypoglycaemia symptoms. Octreotide/lanreotide may raise or lower requirement. Alcohol may intensify or reduce the effect.

src.q: Beta-blockers may mask the symptoms of hypoglycaemia. Octreotide/lanreotide may either increase or decrease the insulin requirement. Alcohol may intensify or reduce the hypoglycaemic effect of insulin.

items.t: GLP-1 receptor agonists: when adding one to insulin degludec, reduce the degludec dose by 20%, then adjust; when adding degludec to a GLP-1 receptor agonist, start at 10 units.

src.q: When adding GLP-1 receptor agonists to Tresiba, it is recommended to reduce the dose of Tresiba by 20% to minimise the risk of hypoglycaemia.
When adding Tresiba to GLP-1 receptor agonists, the recommended daily starting dose is 10 units followed by individual dosage adjustments.

items.t: GLP-1 receptor agonists (MHRA): when one is added to insulin, an insulin dose reduction may be considered to lower hypoglycaemia risk, but reduce insulin stepwise with blood glucose self-monitoring; abrupt reduction or stopping of insulin has led to diabetic ketoacidosis. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not substitutes for insulin.

src.q: blood glucose self-monitoring is necessary when adjusting the dose of insulin, particularly when GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy is initiated and insulin is reduced
Abrupt discontinuation or reduction in insulin doses can lead to poor glycaemic control, with a risk of diabetic ketoacidosis.
GLP-1 receptor agonists are not substitutes for insulin.

items.t: Can be used in renal impairment: intensify glucose monitoring and adjust the dose individually. No eGFR/CrCl thresholds given.

src.q: Tresiba can be used in renal and hepatic impaired patients. Glucose monitoring is to be intensified and the insulin dose adjusted on an individual basis

items.t: Can be used in hepatic impairment: intensify glucose monitoring and adjust the dose individually.

src.q: Tresiba can be used in renal and hepatic impaired patients. Glucose monitoring is to be intensified and the insulin dose adjusted on an individual basis

items.t: May be considered in pregnancy if clinically needed: over 400 pregnancy outcomes show no malformative or fetal/neonatal toxicity. Intensify glucose control and monitoring; requirements usually fall in the first trimester and rise later; adjust the dose individually.

src.q: The treatment with Tresiba may be considered during pregnancy, if clinically needed.
A moderate amount of clinical trial and post-marketing data in pregnant women (more than 400 pregnancy outcomes) indicate no malformative or feto/neonatal toxicity.
Careful monitoring of glucose control is recommended and the insulin dose adjusted on an individual basis.

items.t: UKTIS/BUMPS: insulin can be used in pregnancy to treat diabetes; there are no known risks to the baby. Insulin around delivery can cause short-lived low blood glucose in the newborn, which is checked after birth.

src.q: Insulin can be used in pregnancy to treat diabetes.
There are no known risks to your baby from using insulin in pregnancy.
Insulin use around the time of delivery can lead to your baby having low blood sugar for a short period after birth.

items.t: No clinical experience in breastfeeding; not known if excreted in human milk; no metabolic effects expected in the infant.

src.q: There is no clinical experience with Tresiba during breast-feeding.
No metabolic effects are anticipated in the breast-fed newborn/infant.

items.t: SPS: any insulin can be used during breastfeeding (insulin is a preferred choice); as a precaution, monitor the infant for signs of hypoglycaemia (drowsiness, pallor, sweating or shakiness) and for adequate weight gain.

src.q: Any insulin can be used during breastfeeding, although monitoring is still recommended.
As a precaution, monitor the infant for signs of hypoglycaemia, including drowsiness, appearing pale, or being sweaty or shaky. Monitor for adequate weight gain.

items.t: No adverse effects on fertility in animal studies.

src.q: Animal reproduction studies with insulin degludec have not revealed any adverse effects on fertility.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia: very common.

src.q: Metabolism and nutrition disorders Very common Hypoglycaemia

items.t: Injection-site reactions: common (haematoma, pain, bleeding, redness, nodules, swelling, discolouration, itching), usually mild and transient.

src.q: General disorders and administration site conditions Common Injection site reactions
These reactions are usually mild and transitory and they normally disappear during continued treatment.

items.t: Uncommon: lipodystrophy, peripheral oedema. Not known: cutaneous amyloidosis.

src.q: Uncommon Lipodystrophy Not known Cutaneous amyloidosis
Uncommon Peripheral oedema

items.t: Severe hypoglycaemia can cause unconsciousness, convulsions, brain damage or death. Mild: oral glucose. Severe: glucagon 0.5 to 1 mg IM/SC by a trained person, or IV glucose by a healthcare professional; IV glucose if no response to glucagon in 10 to 15 minutes; then oral carbohydrate.

src.q: Severe hypoglycaemia may lead to unconsciousness and/or convulsions and may result in temporary or permanent impairment of brain function or even death.
can be treated with glucagon (0.5 to 1 mg) given intramuscularly or subcutaneously by a trained person, or with glucose given intravenously by a healthcare professional
Glucose must be given intravenously if the patient does not respond to glucagon within 10 to 15 minutes.

items.t: Immediate-type allergic reactions may be life-threatening; hypersensitivity (tongue and lip swelling, diarrhoea, nausea, tiredness, itching) and urticaria are rare.

src.q: Immediate-type allergic reactions to either insulin itself or the excipients may potentially be life-threatening.
Immune system disorders Rare Hypersensitivity Urticaria

src.q: It is recommended to optimise glycaemic control via dose adjustment based on fasting plasma glucose.

items.t: Close glucose monitoring during transfer from another insulin and in the following weeks.

src.q: Close glucose monitoring is recommended during the transfer and in the following weeks.

items.t: MHRA (high-strength, combination and biosimilar insulins): monitor glucose closely after starting a new insulin product and in the following weeks; doses and timing of other insulins and antidiabetic treatment may need adjusting.

src.q: Monitor glucose levels closely after starting a new treatment and in the following weeks.
You may need to adjust doses and timing of concurrent rapid acting or short acting insulin products and other antidiabetic treatments.

items.t: Subcutaneous injection into thigh, upper arm or abdominal wall; rotate sites within a region. Use a new needle each time (re-used needles block, giving under- or overdose).

src.q: Tresiba is administered subcutaneously by injection in the thigh, the upper arm or the abdominal wall.
Patients should be instructed to always use a new needle.

items.t: Storage: unopened in a refrigerator (2 to 8°C), not frozen. After first opening or carried as a spare: up to 8 weeks, not above 30°C. Pre-filled pen SmPC: may be kept in a refrigerator during this time; cartridge SmPC: do not refrigerate.

src.q: Before first use: Store in a refrigerator (2°C - 8°C). Do not freeze.
After first opening or carried as a spare, the medicinal product may be stored for a maximum of 8 weeks. Do not store above 30°C. Can be stored in a refrigerator (2°C - 8°C).
After first opening or carried as a spare, the medicinal product may be stored for a maximum of 8 weeks. Do not store above 30°C. Do not refrigerate.

src.q: Patients must be instructed to always check the insulin label before each injection

src.q: Patients who forget a dose are advised to take it upon discovery
A minimum of 8 hours between injections should always be ensured.

items.t: Take precautions to avoid hypoglycaemia while driving.

src.q: Patients must be advised to take precautions to avoid hypoglycaemia while driving.

items.t: Carry glucose-containing products.

src.q: It is therefore recommended that the patient always carries glucose-containing products.

items.t: MHRA: cutaneous amyloidosis can occur at insulin injection sites and affect glycaemic control. Remind patients to rotate sites within the same body region; consider amyloidosis when a patient has lumps at injection sites; advise patients to contact their doctor before moving away from a lumpy area (a sudden change may cause hypoglycaemia) and to monitor blood glucose after a change of site.

src.q: remind patients to rotate injection sites within the same body region to reduce or prevent the risk of cutaneous amyloidosis and other skin reactions
